explanations.answer: Flee like a bird to your mountain
explanations.explanation: That's the advice: "Flee like a bird to your mountain!" (Psalm 11:1). David has just said, "In the LORD I take refuge," and then he asks how anyone can tell him that. It's like announcing you're staying put and somebody hands you a map to the exit anyway. The psalm doesn't say who is talking, so I won't guess.

explanations.answer: Hide away in the cave of Adullam
explanations.explanation: The cave of Adullam is a real hiding place in David's life, where he escaped to in 1 Samuel 22:1. But it isn't what this psalm says. Here the advice is "Flee like a bird to your mountain!" (Psalm 11:1). A cave and a mountain are both places to hide, so I can see how they got mixed up.

explanations.answer: Sail away on a ship to Tarshish
explanations.explanation: Tarshish is where Jonah got up and headed when he fled from the presence of the LORD (Jonah 1:3). Different man, different book. In this psalm the advice is "Flee like a bird to your mountain!" (Psalm 11:1). No ship anywhere, friend, just a bird and a mountain.

Right there in the verse: the wicked "shoot from the shadows at the upright in heart" (Psalm 11:2). These are people whose hearts are in the right place, and they're the ones being aimed at. I think that's a heavy picture, and it's okay to let it sit for a second.

Those words don't show up in this psalm. The verse says the wicked set their arrows to shoot at "the upright in heart" (Psalm 11:2). The psalm names that target and no other. I think it's easy to fill in a different group from other places in the Bible, but here we stay with what David wrote.

The widow and the orphan aren't mentioned in this psalm. David says the arrows are meant "for the upright in heart" (Psalm 11:2). Stick with the words on the page, friend. The wicked are in the shadows, and the people they're aiming at are the upright.

The question is, "If the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?" (Psalm 11:3). I wouldn't want my ovens sitting on a floor that's falling apart either. The question hangs there, and then David starts talking about where the LORD is.

Walls are what everybody sees, but the psalm doesn't mention them. The word in the verse is "foundations" (Psalm 11:3). Foundations sit under everything else, which is why losing them is such a big question. The verse asks what the righteous can do if they're destroyed.

The temple does show up in this psalm, but later, in verse 4: "The LORD is in His holy temple." It isn't what the question in verse 3 is about. That question asks, "If the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?" Gates are something you walk through, and foundations are what hold everything up.

David says, "The LORD is in His holy temple; the LORD is on His heavenly throne" (Psalm 11:4). The advice pointed to a mountain, and David points to where the LORD is. He says it twice in one verse, which tells me he wants it to sink in.

Mount Sinai is a real mountain in the Bible, and the LORD came down to the top of it in Exodus 19:20. But that's not what David says here. His words are, "The LORD is in His holy temple" (Psalm 11:4). Funny that the advice was about a mountain and it's still not the right one.

Eden is where Adam and Eve heard the LORD God walking in the garden (Genesis 3:8). This psalm doesn't go back there. David says, "The LORD is in His holy temple; the LORD is on His heavenly throne" (Psalm 11:4). Same LORD, different spot in the Bible.

True. David says, "His eyes are watching closely; they examine the sons of men" (Psalm 11:4). That's a lot more careful than I was with my timer the day I let a batch go dark. The LORD is on His heavenly throne, and the eyes in this verse are watching closely.

The verse says the opposite. David writes, "His eyes are watching closely; they examine the sons of men" (Psalm 11:4). So the statement is true. Notice the two words "watching closely," because David doesn't say "glancing."

David doesn't stop at the wicked. He says, "The LORD tests the righteous and the wicked" (Psalm 11:5). That means both groups are named, so the statement is false. It's an easy one to skim past, friend.

False is right. David writes, "The LORD tests the righteous and the wicked" (Psalm 11:5). Both are named in the same breath. If you only remembered the wicked, I think it's because the verse goes on to talk about the lover of violence.
David says, "His soul hates the lover of violence" (Psalm 11:5). It's a strong line. I think it's one to slow down on and not hurry past.

Money isn't named in this verse. David says, "His soul hates the lover of violence" (Psalm 11:5). The verse names one thing, and it's violence. I think it's worth reading the line slowly so it doesn't get swapped for something else.

Pleasure isn't what this verse says. David writes, "His soul hates the lover of violence" (Psalm 11:5). The word in the verse is violence. Our answer choices can sound close to each other, so it helps to go back to David's exact words.

David says, "On the wicked He will rain down fiery coals and sulfur; a scorching wind will be their portion" (Psalm 11:6). That's a heavy verse, and there's no softening it. Coals, sulfur and a scorching wind are what David names.

That's not what this verse says. David writes that the LORD "will rain down fiery coals and sulfur" (Psalm 11:6). Hail and stones aren't in the psalm. Sticking to David's words keeps the picture the way he painted it.

Frogs and gnats belong to the story of Egypt (Exodus 8:6, 17), not to this psalm. David says the LORD "will rain down fiery coals and sulfur; a scorching wind will be their portion" (Psalm 11:6). Those are the words in this verse. It's a serious line, so I'd stay close to the text.
David says, "For the LORD is righteous; He loves justice" (Psalm 11:7). Those two go together in the same sentence. After all that talk of arrows and fire, this is where David lands.

Riches aren't in this verse. David says, "For the LORD is righteous; He loves justice" (Psalm 11:7). I started out as a 25 cent stamper in a bargain bin, so I'm glad it isn't riches. The word to remember is justice.

Victory sounds like it could fit, but it isn't the word. David writes, "For the LORD is righteous; He loves justice" (Psalm 11:7). The blank is justice. It's the word sitting right next to "righteous."

David ends with, "The upright will see His face" (Psalm 11:7). After the shadows, the arrows and the fire, the last line is about being close to Him. I think it's a gentle way to end a psalm that started with running.
Ruling over the nations isn't in this psalm. The last line is, "The upright will see His face" (Psalm 11:7). David ends with seeing Him, not with ruling. That's the part to hold onto.

Inheriting the earth is a promise Jesus gives the meek in Matthew 5:5. It isn't what David says here. His last line is, "The upright will see His face" (Psalm 11:7). Seeing His face is where this psalm ends.
